name: Pacific Coast Highway (Hwy 1)
description: The crown jewel of American coastal driving. 656 miles of ocean bluffs, sea stacks, and sweeping curves from LA to the Oregon border — with Bixby Bridge as the defining stop.
tip: Drive south-to-north for the best ocean views on your side of the road. Midweek mornings are almost traffic-free.

name: Angeles Crest Highway
description: A rapid climb from the LA basin to 7,902 ft through the San Gabriel Mountains. Genuinely technical switchbacks with almost no traffic — a sports car driver's secret hiding in plain sight.
tip: Check Caltrans for closures after rain — debris is common. Sunrise runs give you the mountain to yourself.

name: Mulholland Drive
description: The ridge road running the spine of the Santa Monica Mountains above Los Angeles. Technical canyon-carving with city views in both directions — a 21-mile proving ground in the middle of a metropolis.
tip: Go at dawn on a weekday. By 9am you share it with Ubers, cyclists, and distracted sightseers.

name: Tioga Pass Road (CA-120)
description: The highest paved crossing in the Sierra Nevada at 9,945 ft, cutting through Yosemite's high country of polished granite and subalpine lakes.
tip: Usually opens late May–June. Check NPS. Tenaya Lake section is worth stopping at every single time.

name: Beartooth Highway (US-212)
description: Charles Kuralt's 'most beautiful road in America.' Switchbacks climb to 10,947 ft through tundra plateaus and glaciers with a view horizon that stretches into Wyoming.
tip: Snow is possible any month at elevation. Fill up in Red Lodge — next fuel is 70 miles away.

name: Going-to-the-Sun Road
description: Carved directly into the Continental Divide at Glacier NP — one of the great engineering achievements of the National Park Service. Exposed cliff edges, waterfalls, and mountain goats at every turn.
tip: Vehicle length limits apply — check NPS. Get there before 9am to skip mandatory shuttle periods.

name: Million Dollar Highway (US-550)
description: Ouray to Silverton through the San Juans: no guardrails on the inside lane, sheer drop-offs of hundreds of feet, and the kind of exposure that sorts out serious drivers from the rest.
tip: This road does not forgive distraction. No-guardrail sections are real — drive the centre line with confidence.

name: Pikes Peak Highway
description: The race-proven ascent to 14,115 ft — site of the Pikes Peak International Hill Climb since 1916. 156 corners, fully paved since 2011, and a summit that is genuinely above the clouds.
tip: Brake fade is a real risk on the descent. Downshift early and use engine braking — your pads will thank you.

name: Independence Pass (CO-82)
description: Colorado's highest paved pass at 12,095 ft between Aspen and Twin Lakes. Exposed switchbacks, thin air, and a summit with 360° alpine views.
tip: Vehicle limit of 35 ft. Altitude affects fuel delivery at the top — give the engine time to adjust.

name: Mount Evans Road (CO-5)
description: The highest paved auto road in North America at 14,265 ft. 28 miles of switchbacks above the treeline with mountain goats literally on the tarmac.
tip: No guardrails above treeline. Afternoon thunderstorms are daily in July–August — summit by noon, no exceptions.

name: Highway 12
description: Utah's Highway 12 threads through Bryce Canyon, Grand Staircase–Escalante, and Capitol Reef — arguably the most scenically dense road in North America.
tip: The Hogsback section is genuinely exposed with drop-offs on both sides. Drive it at dawn for golden light on the sandstone.

name: Moki Dugway (UT-261)
description: Three miles of unpaved switchbacks hand-blasted into the face of Cedar Mesa in 1958. No guardrails. 1,100 ft of exposure. One of the most dramatic short stretches of road in the world.
tip: RVs and trailers not recommended. Descend with low gear engaged — loose gravel on the steep corners is serious.

name: Twisted Sisters (TX FM-336/337)
description: Three farm-to-market roads in the Texas Hill Country that loop through river gorges and ridgelines with tight, rhythmic corners that reward smooth, committed driving.
tip: Leakey is the unofficial hub — fuel, food, and locals who know every mile. Spring and fall are perfect conditions.

name: Tail of the Dragon (US-129)
description: 318 curves packed into 11 miles with zero intersections, zero driveways, and zero distractions. The most famous driving road in America, and it earns every bit of that reputation.
tip: Go on a weekday morning to avoid bikes and cruisers. It's over fast — most drivers go back for a second pass.

name: Moonshiner 28 (NC-28)
description: One of the best roads in the Southeast that almost nobody talks about. 28 miles of technical switchbacks and sweeping bends through the Nantahala Forest.
tip: Less traffic than the Dragon — locals' choice. The stretch from Fontana Dam is the most technical section.

name: Cherohala Skyway
description: The less-crowded sibling to the Tail of the Dragon. 43 miles of ridge-top cruising through the Cherokee and Nantahala National Forests with almost no traffic.
tip: Combine with the Dragon for a full day loop. Cherohala rewards smooth, flowing driving — not trail braking.

name: Kancamagus Highway (NH-112)
description: New Hampshire's 'Kanc' climbs over Kancamagus Pass through White Mountain National Forest. A genuinely flowing road with October foliage spectacle that's hard to match anywhere in the US.
tip: Peak foliage is usually the second week of October. Early morning fog in the valleys creates surreal driving conditions.

name: Smugglers Notch (VT-108)
description: A mountain notch so narrow that boulders literally touch both sides of the road. Closed all winter. 5 miles of switchbacks and blind corners through a gap in the Green Mountains.
tip: Cars over 21 ft are banned. This is NOT the road for wide-bodied sports cars — the clearances are measured in inches.

name: Skyline Drive
description: The ridge road through Shenandoah National Park. 35mph limit, 75 overlooks, and near-zero traffic midweek — one of the most relaxing drives on the East Coast.
tip: Enter at Rockfish Gap (South Entrance) and drive north for better mid-afternoon light on the valley views.

name: Old La Honda Road
description: The Bay Area's legendary sports car road: 10 miles of tight, technical bends between Woodside and La Honda through second-growth redwoods. A short road with a massive following.
tip: Cyclists own this road — they're there every weekend. Find your gap patiently; there is no safe passing on the descent.

name: Tamiami Trail (US-41)
description: Dead-straight slash through the Everglades from Miami to Naples. Zero traffic at dawn, alligators baking on the shoulder, and a road so flat it becomes meditative. Pull over at Shark Valley for a sunrise that will reset your brain.
tip: Leave Miami before sunrise. The golden hour over the river of grass is otherworldly and traffic is nonexistent.

name: Card Sound Road (CR-905)
description: The locals-only alternative to US-1 into the Keys. A sweeping toll bridge over turquoise Card Sound Bay, flanked by mangroves and zero tourist traffic. The best way to enter Key Largo by a mile.
tip: Only  toll. Go early morning — the water turns brilliant teal in morning light and you will have the bridge to yourself.

name: Overseas Highway (US-1) — The Keys
description: 42 bridges stitching together the Florida Keys — ocean on both sides, sky above, and nowhere else like it on earth. Seven Mile Bridge is the highlight. Traffic can stack up but sunrise runs are magic.
tip: Drive south to Key West at dawn, return at dusk — you get the sun behind you both ways and the light on the water is perfect.

name: Alligator Alley (I-75)
description: Perfectly flat, perfectly straight 78-mile toll road slicing through Big Cypress. The road itself is nothing — the experience is everything. Panthers, alligators, and absolute wilderness on both sides at 75 mph.
tip: Pull into the rest area at mile marker 63 just after sunrise. Nothing around you but sawgrass and sky.

name: South Dixie Highway — Homestead Stretch (US-1)
description: US-1 south of Miami through Homestead to Florida City. Opens up into long straights lined with farm stands and nurseries. Not glamorous — but at 5 AM on a Sunday it is wide, empty, and addictive.
tip: Best between 5–7 AM on weekends. Traffic thins completely and the road opens up past Cutler Bay.

name: Krome Avenue (SR-997)
description: Dead straight 40-mile corridor through the agricultural west Miami-Dade flats. No traffic lights for miles. At 5 AM it might be the emptiest road in South Florida. Locals use it to blast between Homestead and Hialeah.
tip: Enter from the south end in Florida City. Pre-dawn is peak — you will barely see another car for 30 miles.

name: Snake Road (CR-833 / SW 8th Ave)
description: A winding two-lane through the Big Cypress semi-wild area west of Homestead. Actual curves — rare in South Florida — with cypress hammocks pressing in from both sides. Light is stunning in the dry season.
tip: Dry season only (Nov–Mar). Wet season flooding can close sections. Zero cell service — enjoy it.

name: A1A Coastal Highway — Fort Lauderdale to Boca Raton
description: Ocean on the left, mansions and yachts on the right. A1A from Fort Lauderdale south through Deerfield Beach to Boca is the quintessential South Florida cruise — especially at dusk on a Friday.
tip: Avoid midday on weekends. Dawn or dusk gives you golden light off the Atlantic and no traffic.

name: A1A — Miami Beach (Collins Ave)
description: Collins Avenue from South Beach north through Mid-Beach and Bal Harbour. Art Deco hotels, palm trees, and Atlantic ocean. More experience than driving performance — but in the right car, at the right hour, it delivers.
tip: Sunday 6 AM — the road is empty, beach crews are out, and the light is golden. You will have Collins almost to yourself.

name: US-27 — Clewiston to Sebring
description: US-27 hugging the western shore of Lake Okeechobee north to Sebring. Long, wide, and smooth through sugarcane fields and small towns. Minimal traffic and surprisingly good surface for its length.
tip: Pair it with a stop at Sebring International Raceway — the oldest road course in the US is a required pilgrimage.

name: Lake Okeechobee Scenic Highway
description: Full loop around Lake Okeechobee — second-largest freshwater lake entirely within the US. Atop the Herbert Hoover Dike, the road gives an almost aerial view of the lake and surrounding marshes.
tip: Ride the top of the dike section between Clewiston and Moore Haven at sunset — nothing around but water, grass, and sky.

name: Old Cutler Road
description: The most beautiful urban road in Miami. A sweeping, winding two-lane under a full canopy of old-growth banyan and live oak trees. Flanks Biscayne Bay through Coral Gables and Pinecrest. Actual curves — in Miami.
tip: Hit it right after sunrise on a weekday. The dappled light through the tree canopy is unlike anything else in South Florida. Low traffic before 8 AM.

name: Bird Road (SW 40th St) to Coral Gables
description: Through Coral Gables into the Gables Waterway area. Mediterranean architecture, tree-lined roundabouts, and low speed bumps — but at 6 AM on a Sunday the roundabouts and sweeping exits are almost car-centric.
tip: Early Sunday mornings only. Explore the maze of Coral Gables streets around Miracle Mile for bonus atmosphere.

name: Corkscrew Road (CR-850)
description: Winding two-lane through cypress swamp and ranch land between Bonita Springs and Immokalee. Genuine bends, dense canopy overhead, wildlife crossings. The most interesting road between Naples and Fort Lauderdale.
tip: Watch for sandhill cranes, deer, and the occasional Florida panther crossing. Drive slowly enough to actually see them.

name: Immokalee Road (CR-846) — East of Naples
description: Wide, freshly paved two-lane from Naples northeast into Immokalee through open ranchland. Completely empty at dawn — stretches of 10+ miles with no traffic signals, no cross streets, nothing but road.
tip: Head east from the I-75 overpass at dawn. You will have a fresh-paved straight virtually to yourself.

name: A1A — Palm Beach Island
description: The narrow barrier island strip of Palm Beach — ocean on one side, the Intracoastal and the most expensive real estate in Florida on the other. A1A here is immaculate, low-speed, and cinematic.
tip: Drive it at sunset heading south. The light off the Atlantic and the mansions behind you is peak Florida luxury.

name: Main Park Road — Everglades NP (to Flamingo)
description: The only road through Everglades National Park, dead-ending at Flamingo on Florida Bay. Sawgrass prairie, mangrove tunnels, and prehistoric-quiet. Sunrise light on the marsh is incomparable.
tip: Gate opens at sunrise. Get there at first light — the low-angle sun on the sawgrass and the guaranteed alligator sightings make it worth the early start.

name: Florida Turnpike — Homestead Extension (SR-821)
description: The cleanest, fastest road in South Florida. SR-821 south from Miramar into Homestead — wide, well-paved, and nearly empty from 11 PM to 5 AM. The de facto midnight cruise route for Miami car culture.
tip: Late night or 4–6 AM is the move. The toll lanes keep casual traffic off and the surface is excellent throughout.

name: Tigertail Lake Road Area — Dade City
description: Dade City sits in the highest elevation of peninsular Florida — the "hills" here are gentle rolls but they translate into actual undulation, something almost nonexistent in the state. The back roads east of town dip and weave through orange groves and old Florida.
tip: Explore the grid of county roads east of US-98 around Lake Jovita. The elevation changes are subtle but real, and traffic is essentially zero.

name: Sugarloaf Key Back Roads
description: The side roads threading through Sugarloaf Key and Cudjoe Key off US-1. Narrow lanes flanked by mangroves, random chickee huts, and total silence. No destination — the wandering is the point.
tip: Leave US-1 and just explore. Turn down any road with trees over it. You will end up somewhere beautiful with your car and zero other people.

name: Little River Canyon Rim Road
description: Follows the western rim of one of the deepest canyons east of the Mississippi, delivering surprise overlooks and tight forested curves above the gorge.
tip: Stop at DeSoto Falls on the way in, then run the rim road south to Canyon Mouth Park for the best canyon views.

name: Cheaha Mountain Road (AL-281)
description: Climbs to the highest point in Alabama through dense hardwood forest with sweeping Appalachian ridge views and surprisingly tight switchbacks.
tip: The summit road beyond the state park entrance has the sharpest curves — take it slow on the way down to enjoy the forest canopy.

name: Lookout Mountain Parkway (AL-176)
description: Runs the spine of Lookout Mountain from the Georgia line to the Tennessee River, combining ridge-top sweepers with forested descents and Civil War overlooks.
tip: The section between Fort Payne and Valley Head has the most consistent elevation changes and traffic-free stretches.

name: Natchez Trace Parkway (Alabama Section)
description: The Alabama stretch of this federal parkway rolls through lush bottomland forest with no commercial traffic, no stop lights, and a perfect 50 mph flow.
tip: Enter near Waterloo and head northeast — morning fog over the creek bottoms makes for an unforgettable drive in spring.

name: Skyway Motorway (Anniston)
description: A short but intense ridge road above Anniston with multiple blind crests, valley pull-offs, and a driving character completely disproportionate to its length.
tip: Best driven northbound in the late afternoon when light comes over the ridge. Very narrow — pull fully off at overlooks.

name: Talladega Scenic Drive (CR-58 Loop)
description: A looping forest drive through Talladega National Forest with continuous directional changes, old-growth hardwoods, and creek crossings that keep speeds honest.
tip: The eastern half between Hillabee Creek and Horseshoe Bend is the most isolated — fuel up in Talladega before you start.

name: Buck's Pocket State Park Road (AL-227)
description: Drops into the Buck's Pocket canyon through a series of blind hairpins before leveling out at one of Alabama's most isolated state parks.
tip: The descent into the pocket is best early morning before traffic. Watch for deer at the canyon floor.

name: Weiss Lake Scenic Loop (AL-9/68)
description: Circles Alabama's largest lake through rolling Appalachian foothills with constant S-curves, lake views, and surprisingly little traffic away from Centre.
tip: Start in Centre and go counterclockwise — the eastern shore road (CR-29) is tighter and more rural than the highway sections.

name: Bankhead Highway Forest Loop
description: Threads through Bankhead National Forest along remote county roads above Lewis Smith Lake with forested ridges, cattle gates, and no cell service.
tip: Check your fuel — the nearest gas is in Double Springs. CR-43 north of the lake has the sharpest turns.

name: Lake Martin Scenic Drive (AL-63)
description: Hugs the eastern shoreline of Lake Martin through wooded coves, crossing multiple creek arms on low bridges with constant gentle curves.
tip: The stretch between Dadeville and Wind Creek State Park is the most consistent for uninterrupted lakeside driving.

name: Coosa River Parkway (AL-21)
description: Follows the Coosa River through the lower Appalachian valley, rolling through small towns and long fast sweepers with the river glittering through the trees.
tip: Best late afternoon — the river catches golden light beautifully. Exit at Gadsden for a food stop.

name: DeSoto State Park Loop
description: Loops through the DeSoto State Park plateau on top of Lookout Mountain, passing the main falls, multiple creek crossings, and dense rhododendron tunnels.
tip: Late October leaf color here is exceptional. The road to the picnic area overlook is the tightest section.

name: Crow Mountain Road
description: One of Alabama's steepest paved roads, climbing Crow Mountain with unguarded switchbacks and exposed ledge sections that reward confident drivers.
tip: Loose gravel on the turns after rain — test the surface before committing speed. Views from the top are worth the climb.

name: AL-35 Fort Payne Scenic Route
description: Sweeps through the broad Lookout Mountain valley between Fort Payne and Centre with long arcing bends, open farmland, and mountain ridge backdrops.
tip: Wide open roads here — perfect for a warm-up run before tackling the rim roads above.

name: Conecuh National Forest Scenic Road (US-29)
description: A long rolling cruise through Conecuh National Forest pine flatlands and creek bottomlands in south Alabama — not twisty, but beautifully isolated.
tip: The Blue Spring Recreation Area turn-off (FR-341) adds 4 miles of tighter forest road for enthusiasts who want more character.

name: Oak Creek Canyon Drive (AZ-89A)
description: Descends 2,000 feet through one of Arizona's most spectacular red-rock canyons on tight switchbacks carved into vertical canyon walls. A legitimate bucket-list road.
tip: Drive top-to-bottom (Flagstaff to Sedona) to feel the full drop. Early morning avoids the tourist traffic that clogs the canyon floor.

name: Mount Lemmon Highway (Catalina Highway)
description: Climbs from Sonoran Desert at 2,800 ft to pine forest at 9,100 ft in 27 miles, passing through five distinct climate zones and 200+ turns.
tip: The zone above Molino Basin has the most aggressive turns. The road ices in winter above 7,000 ft — check conditions.

name: Mingus Mountain Road (AZ-89A, Jerome)
description: Connects Cottonwood to Prescott over Mingus Mountain through the ghost town of Jerome with switchbacks so tight buses must three-point turn them.
tip: Jerome is at the top of the worst section — park and walk through town before descending toward Prescott on equally excellent curves.

name: Coronado Trail (US-191)
description: Nicknamed 'the crookedest highway in the USA' with 460 curves in 123 miles connecting Morenci to Springerville over the Mogollon Rim. A true epic.
tip: Full tank in Clifton — no fuel for 90 miles. The high section (8,500 ft) above Alpine has the tightest continuous curves. Allow 4 hours minimum.

name: Kaibab Plateau Parkway (AZ-67)
description: Cuts arrow-straight through the highest plateau in Arizona before delivering you to the North Rim of the Grand Canyon, with fast sweepers through aspen and ponderosa.
tip: Only open mid-May through mid-October. Morning drives have near-zero traffic and frequent mule deer sightings.

name: Senator Highway (Prescott NF)
description: A historic mining road through the Bradshaw Mountains connecting Prescott to Crown King — paved with embedded gravel sections, tight switchbacks, and 1,000-ft creek drops.
tip: High clearance recommended for the lower section. The views over the Agua Fria drainage from the ridge road are worth the rough surface.

name: Swift Trail Parkway (AZ-366)
description: Spirals up Mount Graham from 2,800 ft desert to 9,700 ft spruce forest through six vegetative zones on a road carved into sheer volcanic cliffs.
tip: The paved section closes at Riggs Flat Lake in winter. The road beyond Shannon Campground is the most exposed and dramatic.

name: Mogollon Rim Road (FR-300)
description: Follows the base of the Mogollon Rim escarpment through ponderosa pine with dramatic rim-edge views, creek crossings, and a completely isolated driving environment.
tip: High clearance recommended — road is well-graded gravel. The section near the Mogollon Campground has the most consistent rim-edge exposure.

name: Sonoita-Patagonia Scenic Road (AZ-83)
description: Rolls through Arizona's grassland wine country with sweeping S-bends over golden hills, mountain backdrop views, and some of the least-crowded asphalt in the state.
tip: The stretch between I-10 and Sonoita is the most open. Pair with AZ-82 through Patagonia for a longer loop.

name: Chiricahua National Monument Road
description: A short but immensely rewarding climb through balanced rock formations and volcanic pinnacles to the Massai Point overlook at 6,870 ft.
tip: Small pullouts — arrive early before the RV crowd. The last mile to Massai Point narrows significantly and delivers the best pinnacle views.

name: Sedona Red Rock Scenic Byway (AZ-179)
description: Winds through Sedona's signature red-rock buttes and spires on a road that seems designed by a landscape artist, with sweeping arc views at every bend.
tip: Sunrise and sunset turn the rock formations deep crimson — plan your drive around the light. Best from south to north (Village of Oak Creek toward town).

name: Yarnell Hill (US-89)
description: Drops from the Weaver Mountains to the Sonoran Desert floor in a concentrated burst of tight switchbacks that compress 2,000 feet into eight miles.
tip: Downhill direction (north to south) lets you see the desert floor view as you commit to each turn. Watch for trucks on the hairpins.

name: Crown King Road (Bradshaw Mountains)
description: One of the most notorious back roads in Arizona — a mining-era road with sheer ledge sections, 1-lane bridges, and switchbacks to the 6,000 ft Crown King area.
tip: Do NOT attempt after rain or in a stock sedan. Passenger-car clearance is the absolute minimum — a sport compact will have issues.

name: Schnebly Hill Road (Sedona)
description: A dirt road that predates Oak Creek Canyon Highway, climbing from Sedona to the Mogollon Rim through some of the most jaw-dropping red rock scenery in Arizona.
tip: High clearance required — no passenger cars below the first switchback. A sport utility or crossover is minimum. The Merry-Go-Round rock formation is a halfway landmark.

name: AZ-260 Payson Rim Run
description: Sweeps from Payson up onto the Mogollon Rim plateau through mixed pine and juniper on a wide, well-paved highway with long fast sections and dramatic rim-edge views.
tip: The transition zone between Payson and Kohls Ranch (miles 260-267) has the best cliff-edge views. Continue to Heber for a 90-mile loop back via AZ-87.

name: Pig Trail Scenic Byway (AR-23)
description: One of the most celebrated driving roads in the South — 19 miles of aggressive Ozark switchbacks named for the hogs that were once walked down this mountain path.
tip: The section between Brashears and Oark is the most technical. Razorback fans run this road in both directions on home football Saturdays.

name: Scenic 7 Byway (AR-7)
description: Arkansas's most famous scenic highway traverses both mountain ranges from the Louisiana border to the Missouri border, with the best driving in the northern Ozark section.
tip: The 45-mile stretch between Harrison and Russellville — through Jasper and the Buffalo River country — is the crown jewel. Allow a full day.

name: Talimena Scenic Drive (AR-88)
description: Follows the crest of Rich Mountain and Winding Stair Mountain on a ridge road that delivers 100-mile views and consistent technical driving through dense hardwood forest.
tip: The Arkansas side (Mena end) has the most concentrated switchbacks. October foliage turns this into a cathedral of color.

name: Boxley Valley Road (AR-43)
description: Winds through a pastoral Ozark valley floor with elk grazing in open meadows, the Buffalo River on one side and towering limestone bluffs on the other.
tip: Wild elk are frequently spotted at dawn and dusk. The 6-mile lower valley section is the most scenic — combine with a Buffalo River bluff overlook.

name: White Rock Mountain Road (FR-1003)
description: A forest service road that climbs to a 2,260-ft summit with 360-degree Ozark views, tight gravel curves, and a complete absence of guardrails.
tip: Gravel road — slow speeds required. The summit has rustic stone cabins rentable by the night for a true mountain sunrise experience.

name: Magazine Mountain Summit Road
description: Climbs to Arkansas's highest point (2,753 ft) through a mixed forest of oaks, pines, and shortleaf pine with a sequence of hairpins below the summit meadow.
tip: The Signal Hill spur (0.5 mi unpaved) adds the 360-degree panorama the main road lacks. Best in late October for foliage.

name: Mount Nebo State Park Road
description: One of Arkansas's most dramatic road experiences — 11 hairpins in 4 miles rising 1,350 feet above the Arkansas River Valley to the flat mesa summit.
tip: The hairpins are numbered 1-11 from the bottom. Hairpins 4-7 are the tightest and most exposed. The mesa top has a 200-mile clear-day view.

name: Cossatot River Road (AR-246)
description: Follows the wild Cossatot River through the Ouachita Mountains with roadside cascades, river crossings, and thick forest hemming tight curves.
tip: Spring runoff (March-April) turns the river a deep green and adds constant sound to the drive. Check for road closures after heavy rain.

name: Ozark Highlands Scenic Byway (AR-16)
description: Crosses several Ozark ridges and creek drainages on a roller-coaster route that locals call 'the switchback highway' — rarely straight for more than a quarter mile.
tip: The section between Boxley and Fallsville has the most concentrated elevation changes. The road through Combs is particularly isolated and picturesque.

name: Steel Creek Road / Buffalo National River
description: A gravel NPS road along the upper Buffalo River with enormous limestone bluffs rising 500 feet directly overhead and river crossings that require confidence.
tip: Check river level before attempting low-water crossings — flooding is common April-May. Erbie to Steel Creek is the best canyon concentration.

name: Hurricane Creek Road (Newton County)
description: A remote single-lane forest road that shadows Hurricane Creek through a narrow gorge carved in the Boston Mountains, with creek fords and overhanging bluffs.
tip: This road is unmarked on many maps — enter via AR-74 near Vendor. Creek fords can be slippery; approach slowly and check depth.

name: Sylamore Scenic Byway (AR-14/5)
description: Follows the North Fork of the White River through the Ozark National Forest with karst springs, river access points, and rolling curves through old-growth hardwood hollows.
tip: Mountain View makes a great basepoint — the folk music scene in town pairs well with an evening drive on AR-14 north toward Calico Rock.

name: AR-21 Buffalo Scenic Highway
description: Crosses the Buffalo River watershed on a series of ridge climbs and creek valley descents that keep drivers fully engaged through 32 miles of Ozark backcountry.
tip: The bridge over the Buffalo River at Rush (turnoff to Rush ghost town) is a worthwhile 2-mile detour onto an unmaintained access road with spectacular bluff views.

name: Mount Magazine Scenic Byway
description: The official byway approach to Magazine Mountain, combining AR-309 and the summit road through a loop that passes Cedar Creek Canyon and the Paris Valley overlook.
tip: Complete the full loop — clockwise takes you past the Cameron Bluff hang glider launch before the summit push. Allow 2 hours minimum.

name: AR-14 Bull Shoals Lake Loop
description: Weaves through the karst-limestone terrain above Bull Shoals Lake on a road full of dips, creek crossings, and abrupt elevation changes typical of the Ozark dissected plateau.
tip: The morning drive from Flippin to Bull Shoals catches the lake fog lifting from the inlet coves. Combine with a boat ramp run to see the water up close.

name: Palomar Mountain East Grade (S7)
description: A relentless climb from desert scrub to 6,100 ft pine forest on a road with 21 numbered turns, banked bends, and the famous Palomar Observatory at the summit.
tip: The South Grade (S6) is the classic descent — tighter and more dramatic than the East Grade. Drive both directions to form a loop.

name: Ortega Highway (CA-74)
description: Cuts through the Santa Ana Mountains connecting Hemet to San Juan Capistrano on a road beloved by motorcyclists for its well-surfaced technical sections.
tip: The 8-mile section through the San Mateo Canyon Wilderness is the most consistent — multiple blind crests keep you honest. Avoid weekends.

name: Glendora Mountain Road (GMR)
description: One of Southern California's most iconic driving roads — a continuous series of technical turns along the crest of the San Gabriel Mountains with LA basin views.
tip: Closed frequently after wildfires. Check Caltrans before going — it reopens quickly but closures are unpredictable. Best driven east-to-west for light.

name: Highway 36 (Red Bluff to Fortuna)
description: Called 'the longest continuous set of curves in North America' by motorcycle touring magazines — 140 miles of relentless S-curves through the Trinity Alps foothills.
tip: Fill up in Platina or Dinsmore — services are 60+ miles apart. The section west of Platina through the South Fork Trinity River watershed is the most concentrated.

name: Ebbetts Pass (CA-4)
description: Crosses the Sierra Nevada at 8,730 ft through volcanic rock formations on one of the most technical state highways in California — narrow, no guardrails, maximum exposure.
tip: The eastern descent from the summit toward Markleeville is the most dramatic — tight switchbacks on a road that feels like it belongs on the Amalfi Coast.

name: CA-128 (Anderson Valley to the Coast)
description: Drops from wine-country valley floor through old-growth redwood canyon to the Mendocino coast on one of NorCal's most varied and rewarding drives.
tip: The final 10 miles through the Navarro River redwood canyon are the highlight — the canopy closes overhead and the road follows every river bend.

name: Kings Canyon Road (CA-180)
description: Descends 5,000 feet into the deepest canyon in North America (deeper than the Grand Canyon) with an unprotected road cut directly into granite walls.
tip: Seasonal — check NPS for exact opening dates (usually late April). The descent from Grant Grove to Cedar Grove takes 45 minutes and requires full concentration.

name: Nacimiento-Fergusson Road (Big Sur)
description: The only road crossing the Santa Lucia Range between Big Sur and US-101 — a nearly forgotten mountain pass with stunning coastal views and a very serious surface.
tip: Frequently closed for slides after rain. One lane through multiple sections — use the pullouts. The western descent to CA-1 is the most dramatic.

name: Rim of the World Drive (CA-18)
description: Traces the entire rim of the San Bernardino Mountains from Cajon Pass to Big Bear, with the Inland Empire spread below and the rim itself delivering constant tight turns.
tip: The section between Crestline and Running Springs has the most consistent curves. Morning drives avoid Big Bear weekend traffic.

name: Mines Road (Livermore to US-101)
description: A back-country corridor through the Diablo Range connecting Livermore to US-101 near San Jose — 50 miles of zero-commercial-traffic mountain driving in the Bay Area's backyard.
tip: The Del Puerto Canyon section (CA-130 continuation) is the finest — narrow road, creek crossings, hawks overhead. Fuel in Livermore; zero services for 50 miles.

name: Guanella Pass Scenic Byway
description: Crosses the Continental Divide at 11,669 ft through one of Colorado's most accessible tundra environments, combining paved switchbacks with an above-treeline final push.
tip: The north side (Georgetown approach) is paved and more technical. The south side (Grant approach) is paved only part-way — the summit view is worth the mixed surface.

name: Poudre Canyon Highway (CO-14)
description: Follows the Cache La Poudre River through a deep granite canyon from Fort Collins to Walden — Colorado's only National Wild and Scenic River road.
tip: The tightest canyon section is between Poudre Park and Kelly Flats. Early spring (March-April) has roaring whitewater and no RV crowds.

name: Kebler Pass Road (CR-12)
description: Crosses an 10,007-ft pass through the world's largest aspen grove on a dirt/gravel road that transforms into a gold tunnel every October.
tip: October leaf color here is legendary — the white-barked aspens turn traffic-stopping gold for 2 weeks. High clearance recommended; passenger cars manage in dry conditions.

name: Cottonwood Pass Road (CR-306)
description: The highest fully-paved pass road in the US Rocky Mountains at 12,126 ft — a beautiful alpine loop from Buena Vista over the Continental Divide.
tip: The road is entirely paved as of 2023. The western descent to Almont (Gunnison) is 20 miles of continuous switchbacks through tundra and krummholz.

name: Ohio Pass Road (CR-730)
description: A high-mountain gravel pass connecting Crested Butte to Gunnison through wildflower meadows and aspens at 10,033 ft — the backdoor to Crested Butte.
tip: Gravel throughout — passenger cars manage in dry weather. The meadow below the summit is one of Colorado's best wildflower spots (late July).

name: San Juan Skyway (CO-145/550/62)
description: A 236-mile loop through the San Juan Mountains connecting Durango, Silverton, Ouray, Telluride, and Cortez — includes Million Dollar Highway and the iconic Lizard Head Pass.
tip: The complete loop is a full day — start in Durango heading north. The Ouray to Telluride stretch via Dallas Divide (CO-62) is the least-driven and most rewarding section.

name: Black Canyon South Rim Road
description: Follows the south rim of the deepest, darkest canyon in Colorado — Black Canyon of the Gunnison — at over 2,000 feet above the river through pinyon-juniper.
tip: Each overlook pull-off is different — don't skip Painted Wall Overlook (highest cliff in Colorado). Evening light turns the canyon walls bronze.

name: Squaw Pass Road (CO-103)
description: A hidden Front Range gem connecting Evergreen to Echo Lake on a high forest road with consistent curves through aspen, spruce, and subalpine fir at 10,000+ ft.
tip: Combine with CO-5 (Mount Blue Sky/Evans) for a giant loop. Less crowded than I-70 corridor — most Front Range locals don't know it exists.

name: Tarryall Road (CR-77)
description: Runs the length of the Tarryall Valley between Lake George and Jefferson through a wide granite-walled mountain valley with zero commercial traffic and 360-degree Rockies views.
tip: Almost no traffic on weekdays. The northern section through the Lost Creek Wilderness approaches opens an entirely different world of granite formations.

name: Flatiron Scenic Byway (CO-93)
description: Cuts between the Flatirons and Rocky Flats on a wide open road with panoramic Front Range views — the kind of road where you just point the car and stare at the mountains.
tip: Afternoon drives catch alpenglow on the Flatirons. Watch for cyclists; they favor this road heavily.

name: Lost Trail Creek / Maroon Bells Road (CO-82 to FR-125)
description: The 10-mile road to the Maroon Bells — Colorado's most photographed mountains — through dark spruce forest to the lake mirror reflecting the 14ers above.
tip: Mandatory shuttle bus in summer (late June-Labor Day). Drive it in shoulder season (Oct or late May) to have the road to yourself — pure alpine perfection.

name: CT-44 Litchfield Hills Run
description: Crosses the Litchfield Hills from the New York border to Winsted through dense hardwood forest on a road that combines consistent S-curves with classic New England scenery.
tip: The Norfolk to Winsted section has the most tree canopy and least traffic. Fall foliage peaks second week of October.

name: Merritt Parkway (CT-15)
description: A 1930s art deco parkway through Fairfield County's wooded corridors — no trucks, unique ornamental bridges at every overpass, perfectly banked curves.
tip: Each of the 68 bridges is unique — no two are alike. The stretch through Greenwich has the best banking and widest sweepers. Trucks banned entirely.

name: CT-41 (Sharon to Falls Village)
description: Winds through the Housatonic Valley's most pastoral landscape, connecting horse-farm villages on a rolling road with stone walls and classic New England character.
tip: Best in spring (May) when the maples are budding or October when the hardwoods are peak color. The Falls Village covered bridge is a worthwhile detour.

name: CT-4 Cornwall Bridge Area
description: Threads through the Cathedral Pines area and Cornwall Bridge village on a narrow forested two-lane typical of the Litchfield Hills — old stone walls, covered bridges, and no commercial traffic.
tip: Cornwall Bridge has an excellent covered bridge — park and walk. The road to West Cornwall (CT-128) is even narrower and more atmospheric.

name: Litchfield Hills Loop (CT-118/254)
description: A pastoral loop through the highest terrain in Connecticut, combining the White Memorial Foundation area, Bantam Lake, and multiple ridge crossings on quiet back roads.
tip: The White Memorial Conservation Center stretch (north of Bantam Lake) has the fewest sight lines and most rolling terrain.

name: CT-116 Norfolk Area
description: Climbs through the highland village of Norfolk — the coldest town in Connecticut — with ridge crossings and maple-canopied lanes typical of the Berkshire foothills.
tip: Norfolk sits at 1,500 ft — it snows when Hartford is dry. Late September drives are excellent when the village maples turn ahead of the lowlands.

name: CT-69/108 Wolcott Highland Loop
description: Crosses the central Connecticut highland between the Naugatuck Valley and Farmington River on a series of ridge roads with surprising elevation and compact farm scenery.
tip: Wolcott is surprisingly elevated for central CT — the ridge between CT-69 and CT-322 has unobstructed valley views that most state residents don't know exist.

name: CT-165 (Voluntown, Pachaug Forest)
description: Passes through the heart of Pachaug State Forest — Connecticut's largest state forest — on a road bordered by pitch pine, Atlantic white cedar swamps, and complete isolation.
tip: The Pachaug Trail crossing area (just west of Voluntown) has the thickest forest canopy. Combine with CT-49 for a full forest loop.

name: CT-49 (Sterling/Voluntown)
description: A forgotten forest road through the Pachaug watershed in Connecticut's quiet corner — completely canopied, hilly, and untouched by suburban development.
tip: The Quiet Corner of Connecticut receives almost no tourist attention. This road on a Sunday morning is as close to empty pavement as CT gets.

name: US-44 Quiet Corner (Pomfret to Putnam)
description: Sweeps through Connecticut's Quiet Corner farming landscape with long views over stone-walled fields, covered bridges nearby, and almost no commercial traffic.
tip: Detour north on CT-97 toward Hampton for even quieter roads — the back roads around Windham County are some of the most pastoral in New England.

name: CT-67 Roxbury/Southbury Area
description: A rolling valley road through Roxbury and Southbury following the Shepaug River with river crossings, old iron bridges, and dense hardwood corridors.
tip: The Shepaug Valley stretch between Roxbury and Woodbury (CT-317) has the best river-road driving — tight bends following every river meander.

name: River Road (Lyme to East Haddam)
description: A narrow tidal-edge road along the Connecticut River's eastern shore through old mill villages and salt marsh, with the river visible through every gap in the trees.
tip: Hamburg Cove (north of Lyme center) is one of New England's most beautiful tidal inlets — worth a slow pass. Road narrows significantly past Brockway's Ferry.

name: CT-9 Chester to Deep River
description: A short but satisfying divided highway section through the Connecticut River valley that transitions to the winding main streets of Chester — one of CT's most charming villages.
tip: Exit CT-9 at Chester and follow the river road (Route 154) both north and south for the actual scenic driving. Chester itself rewards a lunch stop.

name: US-202 Litchfield Green Area
description: Connects Torrington to New Preston through the iconic Litchfield green and White Memorial area on rolling hills with classic New England village centers.
tip: The white-steepled Litchfield green is one of the best-preserved colonial centers in America — worth stopping. The Bantam-to-New Milford section south of town is faster and more open.

name: US-7 / CT-7 Kent to Canaan
description: Follows the Housatonic River from Kent through the Race Brook valley to Canaan, one of the most consistent river-road experiences in southern New England.
tip: Kent Falls State Park is a mandatory stop — the waterfalls are right at the road. The Macedonia Brook area just east of Kent has additional winding side roads.

name: Kennett Pike (DE-52) Chateau Country
description: Cuts through the DuPont family's historic Brandywine Valley estates on a manicured country road flanked by stone walls, horse fencing, and mature hardwood canopy.
tip: Longwood Gardens is at the north end. The stretch between Greenville and Centerville is the most scenically dense — wide sweepers through estate grounds.

name: Brandywine Creek Road (DE-100)
description: A narrow tarmac road hugging the western bank of Brandywine Creek through the same valley Andrew Wyeth painted for 50 years — idyllic, leafy, and traffic-free on weekdays.
tip: The section between Rockland and Ashland has the best creek exposure. Side roads into the Brandywine State Park add a few more miles of wooded canopy.

name: Valley Road (Hockessin)
description: Winds through Hockessin's wooded valley along Red Clay Creek — the most topographically varied road in New Castle County, with modest hills uncommon in Delaware.
tip: The stretch between Brackenville Road and Limestone Road follows the creek closely and has the best natural canopy.

name: Coastal Highway DE-1 (Dover to Rehoboth)
description: The main coastal artery of Delaware's beach resorts — long, fast, and flat with Atlantic horizon views near Rehoboth and a direct ocean connection.
tip: Off-season (October–April) this road empties completely. The Lewes-to-Cape Henlopen section has the best beach access and dune scenery.

name: DE-9 River Road (Wilmington to Port Penn)
description: Follows the Delaware River marshland fringe through some of the most undeveloped land in the state — tidal wetlands, osprey nests, and industrial history side by side.
tip: August and September birdwatching here is exceptional. The road deteriorates slightly south of Chesapeake City junction — worth continuing for the complete isolation.

name: Lancaster Pike (DE-48)
description: A colonial road connecting Wilmington to the Pennsylvania line through the northern Brandywine Valley with stone houses and broad tree canopies.
tip: The section through Centreville is the most intact historically — turn off onto DE-52 for the true chateau country experience.

name: Polly Drummond Hill Road
description: One of the few roads in Delaware with meaningful elevation change — a short ridge-road through preserved open space with valley views unusual for the coastal plain.
tip: Short but genuinely hilly for Delaware. Link with Thompson's Bridge Road for a longer loop through the Newark Country Hills.

name: Smith Bridge Road (Brandywine State Park)
description: A one-lane road through Brandywine State Park connecting to the historic covered Smith Bridge — pure Wyeth-country atmosphere in a state not known for scenic roads.
tip: The covered bridge is accessible only by foot from the closest parking area — but the road to get there is worth the trip for the forested creek environment.

name: Red Clay Valley Scenic Byway
description: A NPS-designated scenic byway following Red Clay Creek through northern Delaware's horse country — one of the few places in the state that genuinely surprises with rural character.
tip: The New Garden Road section near the PA line is the most rural. Look for the historic powder mills along Red Clay Creek.

name: DE-896 / Paper Mill Road
description: Links Newark to Centreville on a rolling road through White Clay Creek State Park — forested, surprisingly hilly, and popular with University of Delaware cyclists.
tip: White Clay Creek State Park has no admission fee. The park roads adjacent to DE-896 are closed to motor traffic but can be walked for views the road doesn't show.

name: Kings Highway (DE-9, Lewes Area)
description: The oldest road in Delaware, connecting Lewes to Georgetown through pine flatlands and farm country with a completely different landscape than the beach resort strip nearby.
tip: Lewes-to-Milton section has the best natural canopy. Combine with a Cape Henlopen drive for ocean scenery on the same trip.

name: Trap Pond State Park Road
description: Loops through the northernmost naturally occurring stand of bald cypress trees in the US — a genuinely surprising environment for Delaware.
tip: The loop road through the park is 1.8 miles but the access road from Laurel adds interest. Canoe or kayak rental available to extend the day.

name: DE-30 Bethany-Fenwick Area
description: A quieter coastal alternative to DE-1, looping through the barrier beach communities between Bethany Beach and Fenwick Island with canal crossings and ocean glimpses.
tip: Delaware Seashore State Park (accessed off DE-1) adds a 6-mile barrier island drive between the ocean and Rehoboth Bay that has no equals in the state.

name: DE-5 / Kitts Hummock Road
description: A county road ending at the Delaware Bay shore through flat farm fields — the Delaware Bay side is nearly undeveloped and has ghost towns of 19th-century fishing communities.
tip: Kitts Hummock itself is barely a village — but the road there through the bay-side wetlands is a completely different Delaware than the resort strip.

name: Centennial Road / Rockford Park Area
description: The most scenic urban driving in Wilmington — roads through Brandywine Park and Rockford Park with valley views, stone bridges, and the Brandywine below.
tip: Drive the full Brandywine Park loop ending at Rockford Tower overlook for the best Delaware River valley panorama within city limits.

name: Richard Russell Scenic Highway (GA-348)
description: A Blue Ridge ridge-top highway considered the best driving road in Georgia — 14 miles of technical S-curves at 3,500 ft with fall foliage that rivals New England.
tip: The stretch from Walnut Fork to Unicoi Gap is the most concentrated. Midweek drives in October are nearly solitary.

name: Wolf Pen Gap Road (GA-180)
description: Crosses Slaughter Gap and Wolf Pen Gap through the Chattahoochee National Forest with multiple switchback sections and the Blood Mountain Wilderness to the east.
tip: The gap between Suches Valley and Blairsville is the most technical section. Combine with GA-60 through Suches for a mountain loop.

name: GA-60 Suches Valley Loop
description: The valley around Suches has been called 'the top of Georgia' — GA-60 loops through a high-elevation farming hollow completely surrounded by mountains, with river crossings and forest tunnels.
tip: Suches is famous among motorcyclists — the loop via GA-60/GA-180 forms one of the best 45-mile mountain circuits in the Southeast.

name: GA-52 (Ellijay to Chatsworth)
description: Crosses Cohutta Mountain on a scenic byway with creek-side curves and mountain passage views — the backbone road of apple-country north Georgia.
tip: The stretch through Fort Mountain State Park adds a 6-mile optional spur. October apple orchards and roadside stands make this a seasonal classic.

name: Brasstown Bald Road (GA-180 Spur)
description: The steepest paved road in Georgia — a 1.2-mile spur with an 11% average grade climbing to the state's highest point at 4,784 ft.
tip: The road is open to private vehicles for limited hours on certain days — verify with Georgia DNR before driving. The 360-degree summit view covers Georgia, NC, TN, and SC.

name: Three Forks Road (Appalachian Trail Area)
description: A forest service road that ends where the Appalachian Trail begins at Springer Mountain — primitive, canopied, and delivering a genuine back-country experience at the famous trail's southern terminus.
tip: Final 2 miles are steep rough gravel — passenger cars can make it in dry conditions. The AT trailhead at the end is the payoff.

name: Betty Creek Road (Rabun County)
description: A narrow mountain road following Betty Creek up toward the North Carolina line — hemlock-lined creek crossings and complete forest immersion on Rabun County's back roads.
tip: Combine with Hale Ridge Road for a full loop through the Betty Creek and Overflow Creek watersheds. Look for Dillard access roads for additional rural character.

name: Warwoman Road (Rabun County)
description: Follows the Warwoman Creek watershed from Clayton to the Chattooga River — a consistently beautiful back road through riparian forest with the feel of a much more remote location.
tip: The Chattooga River at the end of Warwoman is the filming location of Deliverance — wild and isolated even today. Sandy Ford area is exceptional.

name: Tallulah Gorge Scenic Road (US-441/GA-365)
description: The road past Tallulah Gorge State Park crosses a canyon 1,000 feet deep and nearly 2 miles long — the overlook drives off US-441 are brief but spectacular.
tip: The Tallulah Gorge loop (west of the main highway) gives the best canyon-edge driving. The suspension bridge hike requires a permit.

name: Unicoi Gap (US-76)
description: Crosses the Blue Ridge at Unicoi Gap connecting Hiawassee to Helen on a road with consistent elevation change and the Chattahoochee headwaters visible below.
tip: The Helen side is more dramatic — the descent from the gap through the Chattahoochee headwaters is forested and tight. Helen itself is a bizarre Alpine-village tourist trap worth the irony.

name: GA-197 (Clarkesville to Lake Burton)
description: A north Georgia mountain road connecting Clarkesville to the Lake Burton recreation area with forested climbs, narrow bridges, and excellent technical character.
tip: The stretch past Moccasin Creek State Park has roadside waterfall access. Combine with GA-76 toward Clayton for a full mountain day.

name: Cohutta Wilderness Area Roads (FS-18/22)
description: Forest Service roads into one of the largest roadless wilderness areas in the East — rough, creek-crossed, and completely isolated from civilization.
tip: High clearance required. FS-18 (Jacks River Road) is legendary for its 47 creek crossings. Do not attempt after heavy rain.

name: GA-400 to GA-53 Gainesville Foothills
description: The back roads above Lake Lanier through the rolling Piedmont foothills — consistent S-curves, lake glimpses through the trees, and much calmer than the I-985 corridor.
tip: The McEver Road to Browns Bridge Road loop west of GA-400 has the best lake views and least traffic. Morning light on the lake through the trees is excellent.

name: GA-60 South Dahlonega Area
description: Runs south from Dahlonega through the gold-mine country of the Piedmont-Blue Ridge transition with rolling terrain, old stone foundations, and increasing forest as you head north.
tip: The GA-60 northern section from Dahlonega to Suches is one continuous mountain road — combine both sections for a full mountain day out of Atlanta.

name: Fort Mountain State Park Road (GA-52 spur)
description: The short road to Fort Mountain's summit through one of Georgia's best mountain parks — tight curves through oak forest to a 2,850-ft summit with views across Cohutta Wilderness.
tip: The park road continues past the entrance through the camping area to the stone wall overlook — a further 2 miles of forested ridge driving.

name: Sawtooth Scenic Byway (ID-75)
description: Runs through the heart of the Sawtooth Valley between Ketchum and Stanley under the jagged 11,000-ft Sawtooth Range — consistently ranked among America's most spectacular scenic drives.
tip: Stanley sits at 6,200 ft — the valley is often 20°F colder than Ketchum. Drive north-to-south for the mountain-reflected-in-Redfish-Lake moment.

name: Ponderosa Pine Scenic Route (ID-21)
description: Climbs from Boise into the Boise Mountains through massive old-growth ponderosa pine forests to Lowman and the South Fork Payette River drainage — a full day's worth of mountain driving.
tip: Lowman Hot Springs midpoint is worth a stop. The Banner Summit section (7,056 ft) in September is elk rut country.

name: Salmon River Scenic Byway (US-93)
description: Follows the 'River of No Return' through one of the deepest gorges in North America — the Salmon River Canyon averages 5,500 ft of canyon wall from river to ridge.
tip: The section between North Fork and Salmon is the most dramatic — roadside rafters, sheer walls, and zero shoulder. A truly world-class river-road.

name: Teton Scenic Byway (ID-33)
description: Crosses the quieter, Idaho side of the Teton Range through the farming community of Driggs — the same mountains, half the tourists, and a completely different perspective.
tip: The Teton Basin at dawn has the mountains reflected in irrigation canals with zero other cars. Victor to Driggs at sunrise is genuinely moving.

name: Lolo Pass (US-12)
description: Follows the Lochsa River through one of Idaho's deepest canyon corridors on the Lewis and Clark route — 98 miles of wild whitewater scenery with the road carved into the canyon walls.
tip: The Lochsa River stretch west of Lolo Pass is the most concentrated canyon driving — nearly 50 miles with the river always visible below. No services between Missoula and Lowell.

name: Galena Summit (ID-75)
description: The northern gateway to Sun Valley — a 8,701-ft pass with a long approach through the Big Wood River valley and summit views of the Sawtooth peaks.
tip: The descent into Stanley Basin is one of the great mountain drives in the West — the valley floor 3,000 ft below is visible the entire descent.

name: ID-55 (Horseshoe Bend to McCall)
description: Follows the Payette River from the Boise foothills through the steep Payette Canyon to McCall — one of Idaho's most popular weekend drives for its consistent canyon character.
tip: The Banks-to-Horseshoe-Bend section is the tightest canyon. Cascade Reservoir north of Cascade adds a lakeside section. Combine with ID-21 for a full loop.

name: ID-36 Bear Lake Valley Road
description: The scenic valley approach to Bear Lake — a brilliant turquoise lake (its milky color from calcium carbonate) — through Bear Lake Valley farming country on a perfectly smooth road.
tip: The lake's color is most intense in morning light. Paris Valley (north of the lake) adds a Latter-day Saint historic architecture component — Paris Tabernacle is architectural.

name: Lemhi Pass Road (ID-29 to Salmon)
description: A dirt/gravel road over the Lewis and Clark Expedition's Continental Divide crossing at 7,373 ft — rough, isolated, and genuinely historic.
tip: 4WD strongly recommended. The Idaho side descent is much steeper than Montana. Check with Salmon BLM office before attempting.

name: ID-46 Centennial Marsh Area
description: Crosses the Camas Prairie through wetland marshes and high desert sagebrush — extremely open driving through Idaho's most underrated landscape.
tip: Late May brings the camas lily bloom that the Nez Perce harvested — the prairie turns purple. Birding here (sandhill cranes, ducks) is exceptional.

name: Cascade to McCall (ID-55 North)
description: The upper section of ID-55 through Long Valley — a wide mountain valley at 4,800 ft between two ranges with Lake Cascade on one side and the West Mountains on the other.
tip: The 9-mile drive along the eastern shore of Lake Cascade is the highlight — quiet water and distant peaks. McCall's waterfront is the logical terminus.

name: Bruneau Canyon Overlook Road
description: A remote desert road to the rim of Bruneau Canyon — a 800-ft slot canyon that rivals anything in Utah, completely unknown to most visitors.
tip: Gravel road from Bruneau. The canyon is only visible at the rim — the approach through sagebrush desert is monotonous, but the canyon payoff is jaw-dropping.

name: North Fork to Salmon (US-93 South)
description: The southern end of the Salmon River corridor below the dramatic canyon section — the river widens but the road maintains excellent character along the water's edge.
tip: This section has better services than the upper river. The confluence of the Salmon and Lemhi Rivers in Salmon is worth a stop for context.

name: Bald Mountain Road (Sun Valley)
description: A gravel road to the summit of the ski resort's back side — raw alpine terrain, 360-degree Sawtooth views, and zero guardrails above 9,000 ft.
tip: Only accessible when the snow melts (usually late July). The road is rough jeep track near the top — high clearance essential.

name: Salmon River Road (ID-75, Challis to Stanley)
description: The middle section of the Salmon River corridor through the main Salmon River Canyon — technically part of the Sawtooth Byway but the canyon section deserves its own mention.
tip: The section between Clayton and Challis follows the river through a wide granite canyon — midday sun turns the river silver and the walls gold.

name: Great River Road (IL-100, Alton to Quincy)
description: Follows the Illinois bluffs above the Mississippi River on a NPS-designated scenic byway — the road alternates between bluff-top ridge views and river-level bottomland curves.
tip: The Grafton to Hardin section is the most dramatic — pull over at Lover's Leap and Pere Marquette State Park for the best bluff views. Spring flooding can close sections.

name: Shawnee Hills Wine Trail (IL-127/IL-3)
description: Southern Illinois's best driving country — the Shawnee Hills run through the Garden of the Gods and Giant City State Park on roads with real curves uncommon in flat Illinois.
tip: The Giant City State Park roads off IL-51 are the tightest section — narrow bluff-edge roads with sandstone outcrops visible from the car. Alto Pass is the scenic hub.

name: Galena Area Scenic Roads (US-20)
description: Northwest Illinois's hill country — Jo Daviess County escaped the continental glacier and has genuine topography, with Galena sitting in a valley far below the surrounding ridges.
tip: The approach to Galena from any direction is dramatic — the town sits 75 ft below the surrounding terrain. US-20 east of town through the dolomite ridges is the best driving.

name: IL-84 (Great River Road, Savanna to East Dubuque)
description: The northern Illinois section of the Great River Road — higher bluffs and more dramatic river views than the central section, through Palisades State Park and the Mississippi Palisades.
tip: The Mississippi Palisades section (mile 84-94) is the most concentrated bluff driving — vertical dolomite walls rise directly from the road's edge.

name: Giant City Road (Shawnee NF)
description: The road through Giant City State Park through massive sandstone bluff formations — easily the most dramatic short drive in Illinois.
tip: The park road to Little Grassy Lake and the Devil's Standtable is a worthwhile add-on. The bluffs frame the road tightly in both directions.

name: Apple River Canyon Road (IL-78)
description: The Apple River Canyon is the most dramatic topographic feature in northern Illinois — a limestone canyon 150 ft deep that forces the road into real bends uncommon statewide.
tip: Apple River Canyon State Park is directly on the road. The canyon walls are closest at the park bridge — look for the natural arch formation just south.

name: Nauvoo Bluffs Road (Mississippi River)
description: The bluff road above the Mississippi at the old Mormon settlement of Nauvoo — one of Illinois's most historically dense drives with genuine river views from height.
tip: The road wraps the peninsula above the bend where the Mississippi forms an entire peninsula — you can see Iowa, Missouri, and Illinois simultaneously from the highest point.

name: IL-146 Golconda (Ohio River)
description: Follows the Ohio River bluffs through Pope County — the second most isolated county in Illinois — with continuous forest curves above river-level flood plain.
tip: Pope County has no incorporated municipalities outside Golconda. The road from Elizabethtown east along the river is completely undeveloped.

name: IL-178 Starved Rock Area
description: The road through Starved Rock State Park along the Illinois River — sandstone canyons drop to the river on one side while the park's famous canyon system is accessible from multiple pull-offs.
tip: The Starved Rock Lodge area sees the most traffic — enter via Utica and take the back roads through the park for the best canyon access with less crowd.

name: IL-1 (Wabash Scenic Route, East Illinois)
description: The longest highway in Illinois parallels the Wabash River through the flattest, most undeveloped part of the state — not twisty, but consistently beautiful bottomland scenery.
tip: The section between Mount Carmel and Grayville is the most isolated — river-bottom forest with no development for miles. Brilliant fall foliage.

name: Crab Orchard Lake Scenic Loop
description: The loop road around Crab Orchard National Wildlife Refuge lake in southern Illinois — mixed forest and water views on a refuge road with essentially no commercial traffic.
tip: The eastern shore road (Campground Road) is the tightest and most forested section. Bald eagles overwinter here in large numbers (November–February).

name: IL-2 Rock River Drive (Coleta to Rockford)
description: Follows the Rock River through the most scenic stretch in Illinois — Lowden State Park's Eagle's Nest, Castle Rock State Park, and White Pines Forest State Park line this corridor.
tip: White Pines Forest State Park has Illinois's last remaining virgin pine forest — a completely unexpected northern landscape in the Midwest. Combine with IL-64 west for a full river loop.

name: Scenic Ohio River Road (US-45 South)
description: The southernmost tip of Illinois between the Ohio and Mississippi Rivers — alluvial flatlands with bald cypress swamps and the confluence of the two great rivers at Cairo.
tip: Fort Defiance State Park at the confluence is the geographical and emotional endpoint. The cypress swamps along the Cache River to the east are an extraordinary addition.

name: Bishop Hill Area County Roads
description: Rolling farm roads around the Swedish utopian colony of Bishop Hill — gentle hills unusual for central Illinois with an open landscape that emphasizes the sky.
tip: Bishop Hill itself is a National Historic Landmark — the colony architecture is remarkable. The county roads radiating from the village are the most consistently elevated in the region.

name: Alto Pass Scenic Route (IL-127 South)
description: The core of the Shawnee Hills wine and scenic corridor — IL-127 through Alto Pass has the most concentrated bluff scenery and sharpest turns in the Shawnee Hills.
tip: The Bald Knob Cross area above Alto Pass has a ridge road with the best panorama in southern Illinois. The road at dawn with mist in the hollows is stunning.

name: IN-46 Brown County Scenic Route
description: The best driving road in Indiana — IN-46 through Brown County State Park has continuous elevation change, tight forest curves, and the densest fall foliage in the Midwest.
tip: Second week of October is peak foliage — expect traffic. The park road internal loop (IN-135 junction) is the tightest technical section.

name: IN-135 (Nashville to Columbus)
description: Connects Brown County's mountain town of Nashville to Columbus on a winding road through hardwood hollows and creek bottoms with consistent character.
tip: The northern 8 miles from Nashville through Spearsville have the tightest curves and steepest grades — the road levels out approaching Columbus.

name: Hoosier National Forest Roads (FR-1700/1714)
description: Forest service roads through the core of Hoosier National Forest — Indiana's only national forest — with consistent ridge-and-hollow terrain uncommon this flat in the Midwest.
tip: The combination of FR-1714 (Hickory Ridge Road) and the Lake Monroe loop creates a solid 30-mile back-road circuit.

name: Patoka Lake Scenic Drive
description: Loops the western shore of Indiana's second-largest reservoir through forested uplands and creek arms — genuinely hilly terrain in a state famous for flatness.
tip: The western shore road off IN-145 has better topography than the dam-side development. Combine with French Lick for a full southern Indiana day.

name: IN-56 Leavenworth Hills (Ohio River)
description: The Ohio River bluffs of Crawford County offer Indiana's most dramatic terrain — IN-56 between Leavenworth and Mauckport twists through hollows and ridge crossings with real exposure.
tip: The Overlook Restaurant in Leavenworth sits directly on the bluff — best Ohio River view in Indiana. East of town the road has the sharpest sections.

name: Story to Nashville Back Roads (IN-135/45)
description: The back roads between Story and Nashville through Brown County's most isolated hollows — past the legendary Story Inn through dense woodland with zero commercial development.
tip: Story Inn is a genuine time-warp — the general store and inn date to 1851. The roads around the village are the most atmospheric in Indiana.

name: Clifty Falls State Park Road
description: A short but engaging park road over the Clifty Creek gorge area — switchbacks down to the falls and up the opposite wall with canyon views unusual for Indiana.
tip: The canyon rim overlook is accessible only by a park road section closed to regular traffic in summer. Enter early (before 8am) for the full experience.

name: Tunnel Mill Road (Clark County)
description: One of the most locally known driving roads in southern Indiana — a county road through a forest hollow past the historic Tunnel Mill water tunnel and Charlestown State Park area.
tip: Combine with the Charlestown State Park loop road for a 15-mile total back-country circuit south of Charlestown. The actual tunnel is visible from the road.

name: IN-66 Lincoln Heritage Route (Ohio River)
description: Follows the Ohio River bluff country through Lincoln boyhood country — the road between Grandview and Troy has consistent rolling terrain following the river drainage.
tip: The Troy ferry (one of Indiana's last river ferries, to Kentucky) is a worthwhile detour. The bluffs near Rockport are the most dramatic section.

name: IN-246 Spencer Area (Owen County)
description: Owen County back roads through the Hoosier National Forest fringe — gently rolling Midwestern farmland transitions to more forested hollows near McCormick's Creek State Park.
tip: McCormick's Creek State Park — Indiana's first state park — is directly adjacent. The falls trail from the park adds a hike component to the drive.

name: Versailles State Park Loop
description: A park loop road through Versailles State Park — Indiana's largest state park — with rolling forested terrain over Laughery Creek watershed hollows.
tip: The western park loop has the steepest grades. The reservoir dam road (north section) has the best views over the water.

name: Gnaw Bone Back Roads (Brown County)
description: The back county roads around Gnaw Bone in southern Brown County — some of the deepest hollows and sharpest ridge climbs in Indiana on quiet dirt-edged roads.
tip: Combine with Scarce O' Fat Ridge Road for a 15-mile loop entirely within the brown county back country. No signage — bring a map.

name: Big Clifty Creek Road (Harrison County)
description: Harrison County has Indiana's most rugged terrain outside Brown County — Big Clifty Creek Road traces a deep gorge through sandstone and shale hollows toward the Ohio River.
tip: Wyandotte Cave (now Wyandotte Woods State Recreation Area) is accessible from Hwy 62 nearby — the cave tour is one of Indiana's best kept secrets.

name: IN-37 Scenic Section (Bedford to Bloomington)
description: While mostly a commuter road, IN-37 between Bedford and Bloomington crosses the eastern extension of Indiana's hill country with more topographic variation than most of the state.
tip: Exit to Spring Mill State Park (15 miles east of Bedford on IN-60) for the real driving experience — the park road loop is tight and scenic.

name: IN-62 Harrison County Bluffs
description: Between Corydon and Mauckport, IN-62 traverses Indiana's most rugged terrain — the limestone karst of Harrison County with sinkholes, caves, and creek crossings on a bluff-edge road.
tip: Squire Boone Caverns is directly off this road — the cave tour adds cave crickets, formations, and underground streams to the drive.

name: Loess Hills Scenic Byway (IA-183/CR-F20)
description: A ridge-line route through Iowa's loess hills — wind-deposited bluffs rising 200 feet above the Missouri River floodplain, comparable only to the loess cliffs of China.
tip: The section between Turin and Moorhead on the ridge roads (not IA-183) has the steepest grades and most dramatic bluff-top views. Late October brings open landscapes.

name: Great River Road (IA-340, Iowa Side)
description: The Iowa bluff route of the Great River Road — tighter and more dramatic than the Illinois side, with 400-ft limestone bluffs rising directly from the road edge in spots.
tip: The section through Pikes Peak State Park (south of McGregor) and Effigy Mounds is the most dramatic. The road narrows in Marquette — go slowly through town.

name: IA-76 (Lansing Area Bluffs)
description: Northeast Iowa's most dramatic road — IA-76 from Lansing through the bluff country toward New Albin follows the river bluffs through genuine limestone canyon sections.
tip: Mount Hosmer park in Lansing has a road to the top (passenger cars OK) — the overlook above the Mississippi with Lansing below is Iowa's best river view.

name: Backbone State Park Road
description: Iowa's oldest state park preserves a limestone backbone ridge — the park road twists over this unusual feature with steep drops to the Maquoketa River on both sides.
tip: The 'backbone' itself is a 35-ft wide ridge with a 100-ft drop on each side — the road along the top is genuinely exposed. Combine with Maquoketa Caves State Park for a full day.

name: Effigy Mounds Area Roads
description: The roads around the Effigy Mounds National Monument are among Iowa's most scenic — bluff-edge driving above the Mississippi with Native American mound sites and Yellow River forest.
tip: The Yellow River State Forest roads add tight forest curves to this stretch. The combination of IA-76 and the county roads near Harpers Ferry is exceptional.

name: Yellow River State Forest Roads
description: The Yellow River State Forest is Iowa's largest forest — its gravel road network through river valleys and forested ridges offers genuine back-country driving in a very surprising part of Iowa.
tip: The Paint Creek Unit (southern section) has the steepest ridge roads. Gravel throughout — not suitable for sports cars but excellent for adventure-oriented driving.

name: Maquoketa Caves State Park Road
description: A short but engaging park road through Iowa's most cave-rich landscape — the road winds through a dolomite valley with caves visible from the roadway.
tip: The Dance Hall Cave viewpoint is directly roadside — park and walk in. The natural bridge formation is Iowa's most remarkable natural arch.

name: IA-9 (Iowa-Minnesota Border Road)
description: Follows the border bluffs between Iowa and Minnesota through the unglaciated 'driftless zone' — surprisingly hilly terrain with river valley crossings and spring-fed streams.
tip: The section through Decorah (east of IA-9) via the Upper Iowa River is the most beautiful — the river follows the valley floor while the road takes the ridge.

name: Upper Iowa River Scenic Drive
description: The Upper Iowa River valley between Decorah and Bluffton is Iowa's most dramatic inland landscape — 400-ft bluffs, spring-fed streams, and winding valley-floor roads.
tip: The combination of Canoe Road and IA-44 west of Decorah creates a 25-mile loop through the best of the Winneshiek County bluff country.

name: Pikes Peak State Park Road (Iowa)
description: Iowa's Pikes Peak — 500 feet above the Mississippi-Wisconsin River confluence — has a short but superb park road to a viewpoint that some consider the finest in the Midwest.
tip: The confluence of the Wisconsin and Mississippi is visible from the summit at Iowa's Pikes Peak — the only place in the world you can see two rivers this size join from above.

name: Loess Hills South (Council Bluffs Area)
description: The southern end of the Loess Hills — the ridge road network above Council Bluffs through the most isolated section of the hills with open prairie hilltops and sharp descents.
tip: The CR-M38 ridge road above Honey Creek is the most dramatic section — narrow, unlined, and with views across the Missouri River flood plain into Nebraska.

name: IA-27 Harpers Ferry Area
description: The segment of IA-27 through Harpers Ferry and along the upper Mississippi includes the most abrupt bluff-road transitions in Iowa — 300-ft walls and creek-level crossings.
tip: The Harper's Ferry overlook (county road up the bluff) adds the best aerial perspective. The Painted Rock roadside cliff is visible from the highway.

name: Clear Lake Scenic Loop
description: A pleasant loop around Clear Lake on north-central Iowa's most popular recreational lake — rolling moraines and beach-road driving unusual for this flat a latitude.
tip: The south shore road (Buddy Holly Drive, named for the 1959 crash nearby) has the best lake access. The Surf Ballroom in Clear Lake is a music history pilgrimage.

name: IA-150 (Fayette/Bremer County)
description: Northeast Iowa back roads through the Turkey River watershed — rolling farm-and-forest country with the quiet character of Iowa's northeast corner.
tip: The Volga River State Recreation Area (just east of IA-150 near Fayette) adds excellent forest roads to this area.

name: Heritage Trail Dubuque Area
description: The road network around Dubuque through the Mines of Spain area and Swiss Valley — Iowa's most topographically rugged city area with bluff roads resembling western Pennsylvania more than the Midwest.
tip: Dubuque has an operational incline railway (the Fenelon Place Elevator) — the steepest in the US. The bluff roads south of town near the Swiss Valley Forest preserve are excellent.

name: Flint Hills Scenic Byway (K-177)
description: Crosses the last intact tallgrass prairie in North America — K-177 between Council Grove and Cassoday is perhaps the best open-sky driving road in America, waves of grass to every horizon.
tip: Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve is directly on the route near Strong City. April/May prescribed burns turn the hills black, then electric green within weeks.

name: Red Hills Scenic Byway (US-160)
description: Crosses the Gyp Hills — Kansas's 'red hills' where gypsum outcrops and red cedars replace the flat wheat-field stereotype. Buttes, cedar canyons, and Medicine Lodge Valley roads.
tip: Medicine Lodge is the hub — the Peace Treaty site is worth stopping. The Gyp Hills Guest Ranch area has the most pronounced topography.

name: Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve Road
description: The internal roads of the Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve near Strong City — the last remnant of the 170-million-acre sea of grass that covered the continent.
tip: Free admission. The bison herd roams the preserve — they occasionally block the road. June and July bring wildflower diversity that rivals any alpine meadow.

name: Coronado Heights Road (Coronado Heights Park)
description: A solitary outlier butte rising 300 feet above the surrounding plains near Lindsborg — the road to the summit provides the most concentrated topographic experience available in central Kansas.
tip: The view from the top encompass 30 miles of Kansas plains in every direction — genuinely dramatic. The Swedish immigrant history of Lindsborg below is worth exploring.

name: Cimarron National Grassland Road (US-56)
description: Crosses the Cimarron National Grassland — the driest, flattest, and most remote public land in Kansas — with the Santa Fe Trail ruts visible from the roadside.
tip: The Cimarron River crossing area has the most dramatic landscape — a river canyon barely 20 ft deep but impressive in context. The Santa Fe Trail wagon ruts are the best preserved in Kansas.

name: Chase County Scenic Roads (K-177 Loop)
description: The county roads off K-177 through Chase County's cattle ranches — PrairyErth country, the subject of William Least Heat-Moon's most famous book, with limestone post-rock fence posts.
tip: The limestone fence posts (quarried from Permian limestone exposed by erosion) are a uniquely Kansas sight. Spring (April-May) brings wildflowers and calving on the ranches.

name: Kanopolis Reservoir Area (K-141)
description: Kanopolis State Park has the most dramatic landscape in central Kansas — 300-ft sandstone canyon walls near Horsethief Canyon and a reservoir that adds reflected light to the scenery.
tip: Horsethief Canyon trail access is off K-141 directly. The park loop road (Smoky Hill Road) has the best canyon exposure.

name: Big Basin Prairie Preserve Road
description: Big Basin is a 1-mile-wide natural sinkhole in the High Plains — the county roads around it provide some of the most unusual topography in western Kansas.
tip: Little Basin (a smaller collapse nearby) is worth the 2-mile detour. The sinkhole's interior is visible from the surrounding roads — a dramatic geological sight.

name: El Dorado Lake Scenic Drive
description: El Dorado State Park — Kansas's largest — has a network of reservoir-edge roads through native tallgrass prairie and cross-timber woodland.
tip: The northwest section of the park road system has the most wooded canopy and lake exposure. Morning fog over the water in October is beautiful.

name: Maxwell Wildlife Refuge Road
